title: Death inquest for man shot by Regina police set for Aug. 9
subtitle: A public inquest into the death of a man who was shot and killed by a Regina police officer two years ago is set to take place on Aug. 9.
article: A public inquest into the death of a man who was shot and killed by a Regina police officer two years ago is set to start on Aug. 9.

Geoffrey Morris, 41, was killed on May 4, 2019 when Regina police responded to an apartment in the 1900 block of Halifax Street around 5:30 a.m. after receiving reports of a disturbance. According to the Regina Police Service (RPS), officers on scene reported finding a man with a knife holding a woman hostage. Morris was shot later that morning.

The officer who shot Morris was at the time a 14-year member of the Regina Police Service. At a press conference following the shooting , RPS Chief Evan Bray said the officer made the decision to fire his gun because he feared someone could be seriously injured. Bray said police worked for more than an hour to de-escalate the situation before the gun was fired.
The inquest into Morris' death will begin at 10 a.m. at the Atlas Hotel at 4177 Albert St. Coroner Brent Gough will preside at the inquest.
Morris' family has questioned the officer's decision to use lethal force . In a Facebook post written just after he died, Morris' fiancee, Jasmine Brass, said she was present when Morris was killed.
"Honestly it wasn't necessary for them to kill him, they could've just tased him," wrote Brass.
In an interview with the Canadian Press a year after the shooting, Morris' daughter also questioned the actions police took. Kahaila Morris said her father was going through a crisis at the time.
"He was just a human being going through something," Kahaila told the Canadian Press.
In 50 years, Regina police officers have been involved in six previous shootings that resulted in a death.

A death inquest is a public hearing where witnesses are called and evidence is heard before six jury members. Death inquests are fact finding hearings, not fault finding. They are not a civil or criminal proceeding.

In cases of a sudden, unexpected or unnatural death, the Chief Coroner may decide to hold an inquest. Inquests may be held to determine how an individual died or to make dangerous practices or conditions known and make recommendations to avoid preventable deaths.
The jury at a coroner's inquest must determine who died, as well as how, when, where and by what means. The jury may also make recommendations to agencies to prevent similar deaths in the future.
